title: Leafcutter ants don't eat the leaves they carry: they feed them to a fungus farm

cover.alt: Leafcutter ants carrying small green and pale pieces of leaf across bare earth towards the dark entrance of their nest.

body: Leafcutter ants cut fresh leaves and haul them home, but not to eat. The leaves feed a **fungus garden** underground, and the fungus feeds the ant larvae, while the adult ants drink leaf sap. Workers of different sizes split the work: medium-sized ones cut and carry, the tiniest tend the garden, and the biggest guard the nest. These ants fully domesticated their fungus about 15 million years ago.

slides.alt: Leafcutter ants, each holding up a piece of green leaf or pale petal, march up a slope of bare earth and disappear into the dark opening of their nest.
slides.caption: Leafcutter ants carry pieces of leaf and petal up a bare slope and into the dark entrance of their nest.

slides.question: A leafcutter ant can carry up to how many times its own body weight?
slides.explanation: Up to 50 times. Teams of such workers can strip an entire citrus tree in less than 24 hours, which makes some species serious farm pests.

slides.heading: Match each worker to its job
slides.explanation: Workers come in sizes suited to different jobs. Minors are the first line of defence, patrolling around the foraging columns.

slides.label: ants in one huge nest, with mounds spreading up to 80 m
slides.text: Next to humans, leafcutter ants form some of the largest and most complex animal societies on Earth.
